gendered_labor.assessment: UNKNOWN. No Aksumite-period-specific source was found; projecting later, better-documented highland-Ethiopian labor divisions backward onto Aksum would be unfounded inference and was deliberately not done.

political_inequality.assessment: Every securely Aksumite-attested monarch in king lists, coinage, and inscriptions is male; Ezana's own inscriptions name only male co-rulers/relatives. No surviving Aksumite legal text formally excludes women from rule, so "formal exclusion" itself is UNKNOWN — only the observed pattern is documented. Important negative finding: the "Candace"/Kandake queen-mother matrilineal-succession tradition belongs to the separate Kingdom of Kush/Meroë, not Aksum — popular sources conflate them, and this project should not. A claim of "21 queens ruling Ethiopia until the 9th century" traces to later Ethiopian oral tradition/king-lists, not Aksumite-period inscriptions or archaeology, and could not be traced to a primary citation — report as unverified likely later political tradition, not fact.

sources.citation: Munro-Hay, Stuart C. Aksum: An African Civilization of Late Antiquity. Edinburgh University Press, 1991.
sources.author: Stuart C. Munro-Hay

legal_economic_status.assessment: UNKNOWN for the Aksumite period — no surviving Aksumite legal code exists at all. The Fetha Nagast (sometimes loosely cited for "Ethiopian law") is a 13th-century Coptic-Arabic compilation only translated into Ge'ez in the 15th century; applying it to Aksum (already declined by then) would be anachronistic.

sources.citation: General absence of a surviving Aksumite legal corpus, noted across the consulted secondary literature.

household_authority.assessment: UNKNOWN for the Aksumite period specifically. (A separately-dated, better-documented data point exists for the medieval/early-modern Christian-Ethiopian highland period — Allan Hoben, Land Tenure Among the Amhara of Ethiopia, University of Chicago Press, 1973, documents the rist land-tenure system as bilateral/cognatic, giving women independently litigable land claims — but this is centuries after Aksum's decline and is deliberately NOT merged into this Aksumite-period record.)

sources.citation: Hoben, Allan. Land Tenure Among the Amhara of Ethiopia: The Dynamics of Cognatic Descent. University of Chicago Press, 1973 — cited here only to explain why it is NOT used to fill this Aksumite-period gap.
sources.author: Allan Hoben

gendered_legal_restrictions.assessment: UNKNOWN for the Aksumite period specifically. (A separately-dated medieval/early-modern data point exists: Zär'a Ya'ǝqob, r. 1434-1468, undertook documented marriage-law reform campaigns against polygamy; Emperor Menilek II's 1908 decree formally banned polygamy for Christians while he himself practiced it selectively — but these post-date Aksum by roughly a millennium and are not merged into this record.)

dimensions.notes: This record is deliberately UNKNOWN-heavy — it reflects genuine evidentiary thinness for the ancient Aksumite period specifically, not a research shortfall to paper over. Later medieval/early-modern Christian-Ethiopian (Amhara-highland) gender history is a separate, much better-documented topic explicitly not merged in here; it would need its own Culture entity and GenderSystem record in a future research batch.
